name: Fasting spittle

card.summary: A traditional folk remedy of applying saliva produced before eating, usually first thing in the morning, to the skin in the hope of improving blemishes.
card.note: Saliva carries mouth bacteria; no modern trials of the remedy are known.

quick.overview:
Fasting spittle is an old folk remedy in which saliva collected before the first meal of the day is applied to the skin. Folk medicine has used it for skin complaints, which is how it connects to appearance: practitioners hope for clearer, calmer skin without a product.

Saliva contains antibacterial components such as lysozyme and lactoferrin, and some researchers have found growth factors in it, which is the usual starting point for explanations. Whether this translates to benefit on skin has not been tested in clinical studies.
quick.how: Traditionally it is a simple home practice, dabbing morning saliva onto a spot. No standard routine is documented.
quick.risks: Saliva carries oral bacteria and viruses, so applying it to broken skin can introduce microbes. Wikipedia notes it has not been shown that human saliva disinfects wounds.

lead: Fasting spittle is a folk remedy based on applying saliva produced before eating, typically on waking, to skin problems. The practice is old enough to have been the subject of a 1952 article titled 'The fasting spittle' in The Medical Press [1].

Saliva contains antibacterial substances including lysozyme, lactoferrin, lactoperoxidase, thiocyanate and secretory immunoglobulin A. Wikipedia also reports that mouse saliva contains nerve growth factor linked to faster wound healing in a University of Florida study, and that epidermal growth factor is present in human saliva. The same page states that it has not been shown that licking disinfects wounds in humans [2].
People interested in appearance mention it as a no-cost remedy for blemishes. No clinical trials of fasting spittle have been published.

chain: Morning saliva applied to a skin spot
Antibacterial and growth-factor components claimed to help the area
angle.text: Folk users apply it to blemishes hoping to improve how the skin looks. The practice costs nothing and uses what the body already produces.

paras: The name refers to saliva produced while fasting, that is, before the first food of the day. In folk medicine it is applied to the skin. The practice is documented as a subject of historical medical commentary [1].

Human saliva production is about 1,500 mL per day and falls markedly during sleep. Saliva contains thiocyanate, hydrogen peroxide, secretory IgA, lysozyme, lactoperoxidase, lactoferrin and beta defensin, which have antibacterial roles in the mouth [2]. A University of Florida team found nerve growth factor in mouse saliva, and treated wounds healed about twice as fast; it is also present in human saliva [2]. Wikipedia states that licking has not been shown to disinfect human wounds, though it may remove coarse dirt [2].

timeline.event: The Medical Press publishes an article titled 'The fasting spittle' [1].
